 No respite from dengue as winter approaches
 At least 64 deaths, 23,880 hospitalisations in Nov so far 
 Published : 14 November 2026
 • 
 Updated : 14 November 2026, 02:41
 • 
 BANGLADESH
 SHARE 
 Helemul Alam
 Helemul Alam 
 At least 64 people died of dengue and 23,880 others were hospitalised in the first 13 days of November, as the outbreak continues to take a heavy toll towards the end of the year.
 Experts warn that the situation could remain severe throughout November, with December likely to see more cases than in previous years.
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), dengue claimed 174 lives in October, 148 in September, 43 in August, 36 in July and 13 in June.
 Hospitalisations stood at around 53,000 in October, 43,774 in September, 20,536 in August, 9,206 in July and 2,907 in June.
 Prof Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University’s Department of Zoology said the outbreak might not subside as quickly as previously expected, particularly due to recent rainfall, including rain two days ago.
 Based on current trends, the decline in dengue cases during November could be smaller than initially anticipated, he said.
 Bashar, an entomologist, stressed the need to eliminate mosquito breeding grounds, warning that rainfall could create new breeding sites wherever water accumulates.
 He recommended applying larvicide where stagnant water could not be removed and regularly monitoring potential breeding sites to control the Aedes mosquito population.
 He also called for stronger measures against Culex mosquitoes, whose population is likely to increase in the coming days.
 HM Nazmul Ahsan, associate professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, said although dengue cases had declined slightly, hospitals were still receiving a considerable number of critically ill patients.
 Ahsan warned that delays in transportation, emergency assessment and hospital admission could cause irreversible organ damage and increase the risk of death among patients with dengue shock.
 Early treatment, however, significantly improves their chances of recovery, he said.
 He also reported severe complications among dengue patients this year, including liver, kidney, respiratory and heart failure, as well as myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle.
 Such complications appeared more common than in previous years, although further studies were needed to determine the reasons, he added.
 Ahsan said the circulation of dengue virus serotype 3 (DENV-3) could be a contributing factor, as variations within a serotype may influence disease severity.
 He urged high-risk patients, including those with heart, lung, liver or kidney diseases, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or obesity, to seek hospital admission promptly after diagnosis.
 “Early hospitalisation is our main recommendation, particularly for high-risk patients. If we can reduce delays in seeking care and ensure appropriate treatment and stabilisation, we may be able to reduce the number of deaths and severe outcomes,” Nazmul said.
